title: They're people
hookLine: "they're slaves" "no, they're people, they're housemates, humble friends" (Letters 47)

lines: A ROMAN DINNER, SERVED IN SILENCE.
cards: A Roman dinner party. The master reclines and eats more than he can hold. Around the couches, enslaved people stand all night, silent and hungry.
One clears up what the drunken guests have spilled. One carves. One pours the wine.
If any of them so much as coughs or hiccups, Seneca says, there's a beating. A few days ago this path promised to look straight at this, and the forty-seventh letter is where Seneca himself does.
It opens with a little argument, as if someone kept interrupting him.

teach.b: Someone says: they're slaves. Seneca answers: no, they're people. Slaves!
No, housemates. Slaves! No, humble friends.
Slaves! No, fellow slaves, if you remember that fortune has the same power over all of us. Four replies, each one closing the distance.
The one you call a slave, he says, was born of the same seeds, enjoys the same sky, breathes, lives and dies as you do. You could see him free; he could see you enslaved.
Romans had a proverb: so many slaves, so many enemies.
Seneca's answer: we don't have them as enemies; we make them so, by cruelty. Now the honest part. Seneca never called for slavery to end.

He owned many enslaved people himself, and his great household ran on their labor. His letter asks masters to be humane, to eat with those they trust, to talk with them. It doesn't ask them to let go.
Both things are true: this letter is often counted among the most humane Roman writings on slavery, and it stops far short of freedom.

Looking back on the week, from the rich man's library to the god within, this is where Seneca's large ideas meet a real dinner table. The divine in every mind has to include the person pouring the wine.

how: Many people who read this letter make a habit of learning and using the names of those who serve them, and of thanking them directly.

o: Seneca's answer to 'slaves': they are human beings
a word for the citizens who could vote in Rome
a Roman name for the paid staff of a household

games.q: the forty-seventh letter — tap the pairs.
p: so many slaves, so many enemies

s: Seneca called for slavery to be abolished
he asked masters to be humane, but never called for an end to slavery.
Seneca says enslaved people are born of the same seeds as their masters
same sky, same breath, same life and death.
Seneca accepts the proverb that every slave is an enemy
he says masters make them enemies through cruelty.

games.q: you're at a Roman dinner. a guest says, of the silent servers, 'they're slaves.' what does Seneca reply first?
games.why: Seneca answers four times: people, housemates, humble friends, fellow slaves under the same fortune.

practice: Think of the people who served you this past week whose names you may not know: a cashier, a driver, a cleaner, someone who cooked your food. Picture one face as clearly as you can: same sky, same breath, same short life.
If you know their name, say it silently; if you don't, notice that, without blame.

wordCard.voice: They're people. Seneca's forty-seventh letter answers 'slaves' four times: people, housemates, humble friends, fellow slaves. Humane, and still short of freedom. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, Seneca, Letters 47.1: they're slaves. No, they're human beings.
